prime.problem: "Design a parking lot" goes wrong when rules land on the wrong class (a vehicle checking every spot type, 12 cases over 3 classes) or the policy is baked into one method, so trying best-fit instead of first-fit means rewriting the lot.
prime.fits: Last OOD card: it uses everything before it. Classes and frozen values, inheritance (Car is a Vehicle), interfaces (a policy is anything callable), and the requirements card's clarifying questions, which decide the classes.
expect: put the rule with the data it reads (spot.fits)
which round you're in (OOD vs system design)
prime.goal: Turn an OOD prompt into a small class sketch with each rule on the class that owns its data and each swappable choice passed in, and justify it with a trace.

attend: Why does fits(vehicle) belong on Spot rather than on Vehicle?
In the six-arrival trace, which single early choice makes first-fit reject bus y?
How does passing choose=best_fit change the design compared with an if/elif inside park?
Why does Fisher–Yates give every order probability exactly 1/n!, and why can't the naive "swap with randrange(n)" be fair?
What does the card say an OOD round wants, compared with a system-design round?

must: Put each rule in the class that owns the data it reads → a spot knows its size, so spot.fits(v) is one comparison of sizes → a new vehicle or spot kind changes one place, not 3 × 4 cases
Pass swappable behaviour in (strategy/policy) → ParkingLot(choose=best_fit) → changing first-fit to best-fit changes the outcome (5 of 6 → 6 of 6) without editing any class

Fisher–Yates: at step i pick j uniformly in 0…i and swap → position i is final → n · (n−1) ⋯ 1 equally likely paths map one-to-one onto n! orders → uniform; the naive loop's nⁿ paths can't split evenly over n! orders
Clarifying questions → decide the classes (levels? vehicle types? permits?) → and the round decides the altitude: classes and methods for OOD, APIs, storage and scale for system design
elevated: A seeded RNG passed into shuffle(rng) → the same shuffle every test run; and a 32-bit seed reaches at most ≈ 4.29 × 10⁹ of 52! ≈ 8.07 × 10⁶⁷ orders → for a real card game the seed, not the loop, is the weak point
reference: the sketches for jukebox, chess, jigsaw, chat, Othello, file system and GC

compress.prompt: From memory, sketch the parking lot's classes with their relations (has-a, is-a, enum, policy), write fits as one expression, and state the rule "rule with the data, policy passed in" in your own words. Then write Fisher–Yates in four lines.
checklist: ParkingLot has Levels has Spots; Car/Bus/Motorcycle is a Vehicle; Size is an enum
fits: spot free, vehicle size ≤ spot size, accessible only with a permit
the choosing policy is a function passed in
Fisher–Yates walks down from the last position, swapping with a uniform j ≤ i
use classes when data and rules travel together; otherwise plain data

retrieve.q: Explain "put the rule with the data it reads" using what happens when a new spot kind (say, a motorcycle-only bay) is added under each design.
answer: rule on Spot: one new spot size or flag, fits maybe one clause
rule on each Vehicle with isinstance checks: every vehicle class must be edited
the owner of the data is the one place that has to change

retrieve.q: Trace the first two arrivals (two compact cars) under first-fit and best-fit on the card's lot: which spots are candidates and which is picked?
answer: first-fit: car a sees L1 C1 L2 C2 → L1; car b sees C1 L2 C2 → C1
best-fit: car a → C1 (smallest that fits); car b sees L1 L2 C2 → C2
first-fit has already spent a large spot on a car, which later costs bus y

retrieve.q: An interviewer asks you to "design a chat server". Should you start with a class diagram? What does the card say about choosing the altitude?
answer: depends on the round: OOD wants classes, relations and a method or two
system design wants APIs, storage and scale; a class diagram is the wrong altitude
either way ask the clarifying questions first

retrieve.q: Why does "swap a[i] with a[randrange(n)]" bias a 3-card shuffle, and what are the counts?
answer: 27 / 6 = 4.5 isn't whole, so some orders must get more paths
counts 4, 5, 5, 5, 4, 4 out of 27; Fisher–Yates gives 1 each out of 6

compare.q: Passing choose into ParkingLot and passing state into shorten are both "pass it in, don't hardwire it". What does each one make swappable or testable, and what would the hardwired version cost?
answer: the policy can be swapped (first-fit vs best-fit) without editing the lot
the state can be any literal, so one call tests any case
hardwired: edit and retest the lot for each policy; replay history for each test

compare.q: Fisher–Yates and the blacklist random-pick card both need every outcome equally likely. What mechanism guarantees uniformity in each, and what bug breaks it?
answer: Fisher–Yates: each step picks uniformly among the positions still unfixed, giving n! equally likely paths
blacklist pick: draw uniformly from [0, m) and remap each hole to a distinct allowed value
bugs: picking from the whole range each step, or a remap that sends two draws to the same value

predict.q: Before computing: with the naive "swap with randrange(n)" shuffle on 4 cards, is the bias worse or better than on 3? Guess the fewest and the most paths any single order gets out of 4⁴ = 256.
predict.answer: Worse. 256 paths onto 24 orders is 10.67 each on average, and the real counts range from 8 to 15 paths per order (enumerated by a short script). The most likely order is almost twice as likely as the least likely one. On 3 cards the range was only 4 to 5.

apply.task: Implement the call-centre prompt from the card's table: Employee(name, rank), Call(level) and a Dispatcher.get_call_handler(call) that returns the lowest-ranked free employee at or above the call's level, or queues the call if nobody is free. Staff: 2 freshers, 1 team leader, 1 project manager. Replay: 3 level-0 calls arrive while nobody hangs up, then 1 level-2 call.
apply.done: The first two calls go to the two freshers, the third goes to the team leader, and the level-2 call goes to the project manager. A fifth call of any level is queued. No class other than Dispatcher contains the escalation rule.
apply.hint: Keep employees in a list sorted by rank and scan for the first free one whose rank ≥ call.level.

reflect: Which prediction did you get wrong: how the naive shuffle's bias grows with n?
What couldn't you explain cleanly: why the policy is a parameter rather than a subclass?
Which relationship is still fuzzy: data owner → where the rule lives, or clarifying question → which classes exist?
Which of the nine other prompts could you sketch in five minutes, and which not yet?
What will you look for in the estimation part: whether your design fits once numbers arrive?
